title: 1 Samuel 5:6–12
context: The LORD’s hand is heavy on Ashdod, striking the people with tumors, so they send the ark to Gath, where the LORD’s hand brings panic and tumors, and then to Ekron, whose people cry out that the ark will kill them. The lords of the Philistines agree to send the ark back to its place, as the cry of the city goes up to heaven. Both traditions read this as shared ground on God’s holiness and power over the nations, and the nature of the affliction is uncertain.

verses.text: But the LORD’s hand was heavy on the people of Ashdod, and he destroyed them and struck them with tumors, even Ashdod and its borders.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s hand is heavy on Ashdod; he destroys them and strikes them with tumors. Arminian readers note God acting directly against the city that holds his ark.

The exact nature of the tumors is uncertain, and translations and interpreters differ.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s judgment on the Philistines, recalled in Psalm 78:66.

The phrase “the LORD’s hand” echoes the language of the plagues on Egypt (Exod 9:3).

verses.text: When the men of Ashdod saw that it was so, they said, “The ark of the God of Israel shall not stay with us, for his hand is severe on us and on Dagon our god.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of Ashdod say the ark of the God of Israel must not stay, for his hand is severe on them and on Dagon. Arminian readers note that they rightly connect their suffering with the ark.

They recognize a power greater than their god.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the nations compelled to acknowledge the LORD’s power.

Their confession that his hand is severe “on Dagon our god” admits Dagon’s defeat in their own words.

verses.text: They sent therefore and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines, and said, “What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?” They answered, “Let the ark of the God of Israel be carried over to Gath.” They carried the ark of the God of Israel there.
verses.arminianNotes:
The lords of the Philistines gather and decide to carry the ark to Gath. Arminian readers note the attempt to solve the problem by moving it.

They hope a different city will escape the judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see human strategies failing against God.

Moving the ark only spreads the judgment, showing that God’s holiness cannot be managed by political decisions.

verses.text: It was so, that after they had carried it there, the LORD’s hand was against the city with a very great confusion; and he struck the men of the city, both small and great, so that tumors broke out on them.
verses.arminianNotes:
In Gath the LORD’s hand brings very great confusion, and tumors break out on small and great alike. Arminian readers note that the same judgment follows the ark.

The repetition makes the cause unmistakable.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty displayed city by city.

No place can contain or tame his holiness, and the judgment falls on all classes, “both small and great.”

verses.text: So they sent God’s ark to Ekron. As God’s ark came to Ekron, the Ekronites cried out, saying, “They have brought the ark of the God of Israel here to us, to kill us and our people.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They send God’s ark to Ekron, and the Ekronites cry out that it has been brought to kill them. Arminian readers note that word of the judgment has spread before the ark arrives.

Ekron fears death the moment the ark enters.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see escalating terror as the ark moves through Philistia.

The nations now recognize the danger of holding the LORD’s ark. Their fear contrasts with Israel’s earlier presumption in 4:3.

verses.text: They sent therefore and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines, and they said, “Send the ark of the God of Israel away, and let it go again to its own place, that it not kill us and our people.” For there was a deadly panic throughout all the city. The hand of God was very heavy there.
verses.arminianNotes:
The lords agree to send the ark back to its own place, for a deadly panic fills the city and God’s hand is very heavy there. Arminian readers note that the Philistines finally decide to return what they took.

The decision comes from fear rather than faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God compelling the return of his ark without any Israelite army.

The LORD vindicates his own name. The narrative moves toward the ark’s return in chapter 6.

verses.text: The men who didn’t die were struck with the tumors; and the cry of the city went up to heaven.
verses.arminianNotes:
Those who did not die were struck with tumors, and the cry of the city went up to heaven. Arminian readers note the depth of the suffering.

The cry recalls the great cry in Egypt at the last plague (Exod 12:30).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see judgment and lament together.

The chapter ends with the LORD’s victory over the Philistines’ god, which both traditions read as shared ground about God’s holiness and power.
